title: Daniel in the Den of Lions
summary: Under Darius, Daniel rises so high that jealous officials plot against him, persuading the king to forbid prayer to anyone but himself for thirty days. Daniel keeps praying toward Jerusalem three times a day, is thrown to the lions, and is found unharmed in the morning because God sent his angel. His accusers are destroyed, and Darius decrees that all his kingdom must fear the living God of Daniel.
story: The kingdom has passed from Babylon to the Medes and Persians, but the situation of God's people has not changed: they still live under a foreign king whose laws can turn against them. Daniel, now past eighty if the book's dates are followed, serves a new regime with the same integrity he showed under Nebuchadnezzar. This is the last of the court stories, and it pairs with chapter 3. There the test was a command to do what God forbids; here it is a command not to do what God requires. Both end with deliverance and a royal decree honoring God. Darius's confession that God's "kingdom will never be destroyed" (verse 26) echoes chapter 2 and prepares for the visions of chapter 7, where that kingdom is given to the Son of Man.
historical:
The chapter is set in the reign of Darius the Mede, who received the kingdom when Babylon fell in 539 BC (5:31). This figure is not known by that name outside Daniel, and his identity is one of the book's historical puzzles (see the hard question). The administrative picture fits Persian rule. The Persians governed through satraps, provincial governors, with other officials under and around them. Herodotus counts about twenty satrapies in the time of Darius I, so the 120 satraps of verse 1 are often taken as a broader term for regional officials; Esther 1:1 speaks of 127 provinces.

The principle that a royal decree could not be revoked appears also in Esther (1:19; 8:8), described there as a law of Persia and Media. No Persian source states such a rule in these words, and some think it reflects a court custom of the king's word being final rather than a written law. Lions were kept by Near Eastern kings; Assyrian palace reliefs show royal lion hunts with lions released from cages, and kings displayed their power by controlling these animals.
cultural:
Daniel prays in an upper room with windows open toward Jerusalem. Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication had asked God to hear his people when they prayed toward the land, the city, and the temple from the land of their captivity (1 Kings 8:46-49), and Daniel does exactly that, though the temple lies in ruins. Praying three times a day matches Psalm 55:17 and became Jewish practice, later tied to the times of the temple's daily sacrifices. Kneeling and giving thanks are both noted: Daniel's prayer under threat still includes thanksgiving.

The decree asks all subjects to petition only the king for thirty days. Such a law would treat the king as the sole channel to the divine, and the officials knew that Daniel's faithfulness was the one place they could catch him (verse 5). The punishment of the accusers together with their wives and children (verse 24) reflects a practice of collective punishment known in the ancient world, which the Law of Moses forbade for Israel's own courts (Deuteronomy 24:16). The narrator reports it as Persian justice, not as a model.
literary: The story is built on a series of reversals. The officials seek a charge against Daniel and find none except his faithfulness to God. The king who signs the decree then labors until sundown to save the man it condemns. The stone and seals meant to make sure nothing about Daniel could change instead preserve the evidence of his deliverance. The accusers fall into the pit they dug. Repetition carries the tension: the law of the Medes and Persians is mentioned three times, each time closing another exit. The king's anguished question at dawn (verse 20) is answered by Daniel's calm greeting, and the chapter ends with a decree whose poetry (verses 26 to 27) restates the book's central confession in the mouth of a Persian king.

outline.t: Daniel's excellence and the officials' plot
Daniel prays as before and is accused
Into the den and a sleepless night for the king
Delivered at dawn and the accusers punished

doctrines.note: Daniel's prayer life is the whole issue of the chapter. He prays as he always had, openly and regularly, with thanksgiving, and he does not change the habit to avoid danger or to make a show of defiance.
Daniel was lifted out unharmed "because he had trusted in his God" (verse 23). Hebrews 11:33 remembers those who through faith "shut the mouths of lions".
The chapter ends with a Persian king confessing that God's kingdom will never be destroyed and his dominion will never end. Earthly laws that cannot be changed prove weaker than the God who rescues.

words.note: Dat, law or decree, a word borrowed from Persian. The chapter plays on two laws: the law of Daniel's God (verse 5) and the law of the Medes and Persians. The story is about what happens when they collide.
Esar, a binding decree or injunction, used for the prohibition the king signs. It comes from a root meaning to bind, and the whole plot turns on how tightly the king has bound himself.
Chay, living. Darius calls Daniel's God "the living God" (verses 20 and 26), in contrast to the idols of metal and wood that cannot see or hear (5:23). The living God acts in the world and rescues.
Shezav, to deliver or rescue, a key word in both chapter 3 and this chapter. Darius hopes Daniel's God will deliver him (verse 16) and at the end confesses that he delivers and rescues (verse 27).

christ: Early Christians saw in this chapter a picture of Jesus' death and resurrection. Daniel is innocent, condemned by the envy of officials under a law the ruler cannot overturn, placed in a pit sealed with a stone, and found alive when the ruler comes at the first light of dawn. The Gospels describe Jesus' tomb as secured "by sealing the stone and posting the guard" (Matthew 27:66), and the women coming very early in the morning. The resemblance is a pattern, not a prophecy, and the difference matters as much as the likeness: Daniel was kept from death, while Jesus went into death and came out of it. The chapter's confession of the "living God" whose kingdom will never end finds its fullest meaning in the risen Christ.

hard.a: No ancient source outside Daniel names a Darius the Mede who ruled Babylon after its fall, and the known Persian kings named Darius come later. Several explanations are offered. Some identify him with an official under Cyrus named in Babylonian records: either Ugbaru, the general whose army took the city and who died a few weeks later, or Gubaru, whom Cyrus placed over Babylon to appoint its officials. Others, following a proposal by the scholar D. J. Wiseman, identify him with Cyrus himself and translate 6:28 as in the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus the Persian. Many critical scholars regard him as a literary figure formed from traditions about the later Darius I and from the prophetic expectation that the Medes would conquer Babylon (Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11), which fits the four-kingdom scheme of Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece. None of these views has won general agreement. The chapter's message does not depend on the solution: God's servant is kept safe under a new empire as under the old.

questions: Daniel's enemies could find nothing against him except his faithfulness to God. What would people have to look at to find something against you?
Daniel neither hid his prayers nor staged a protest; he prayed "just as he had done before". What habits of faith in your life would continue unchanged under pressure?
Darius was trapped by his own law. How do people with power get caught by the systems they create, and what does that suggest about trusting any human authority completely?
